Empirical Research Plan: “Educational Interventions and Student Achievement”

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
Chosen method: Staggered Difference-in-Differences (DID) with an event-study
parameterization.

Why appropriate  
• The intervention was rolled out to different schools in different years ⇒
exogenous time- and cross-sectional variation.  
• Annual panel of the same students ⇒ we can observe outcomes both before and
after treatment for each cohort.  
• Modern staggered-adoption DID estimators (Callaway–Sant’Anna 2021; Sun &
Abraham 2021) deliver unbiased average treatment effects and dynamic
coefficients even when treatment timing differs.

We will complement the DID with (i) an event-study to trace dynamics and (ii)
heterogeneity analyses by grade, gender and baseline achievement.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable  
Treated_it = 1 if student i attends a school that has implemented the reform
by school-year t, and 0 otherwise.

Control group (counterfactual)  
Students in schools that have not yet implemented the intervention in year t.
Schools that never adopt remain pure controls.

Treatment timing / event date  
For every school s we record AdoptionYear_s.  
Event time k = t – AdoptionYear_s (k = 0 is the first treated year).

No RDD running variable is needed because we employ DID.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Parallel Trends (Conditional)  
In absence of the reform, average test-score growth in treated and
not-yet-treated schools would have evolved similarly.  
Plausibility: Roll-out allegedly driven by administrative capacity, not recent
test trends. We can inspect pre-trends and include school-specific linear
trends.

A2. No Anticipation  
Students and teachers do not change behaviour in advance of the official
start date.  
Plausibility: Curriculum materials/trainings delivered close to adoption → low
scope for early response; will test by estimating coefficients for k = –2, –3.

A3. Stable Composition  
Student composition within a school is not differentially changing because of
the program.  
Plausibility: Most U.S. public-school districts have constrained mobility, but
we will verify by comparing inflow/outflow patterns.

A4. No Spillovers (SUTVA)  
Outcomes of control students are not affected by neighbouring schools’ early
adoption.  
Plausibility is moderate; we will explore geographic spillover specifications.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  

T1. Non-random adoption timing  
If low-performing schools were prioritized, estimates may mix treatment with
mean-reversion. Mitigation:  
• Include school fixed effects, year fixed effects, and pre-treatment mean
scores.  
• Instrument adoption timing with the district’s original administrative
schedule (if available).  
• Event-study pre-trend test.

T2. Student Sorting / Attrition  
Parents could transfer children into reform schools. Mitigation:  
• Track individual students; restrict to stayers; re-weight with inverse
probability weights for staying.  
• Show robustness using school-by-cohort aggregates (less sensitive to
individual moves).

T3. Spillovers across nearby schools  
Mitigation:  
• Include indicators for proportion of neighbouring schools already treated.  
• Cluster standard errors at the district level and perform leave-one-district-
out robustness.  
• Alternative specification dropping schools within X miles of early adopters.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
5. R CODE OUTLINE (executable)

```r
# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 0. Packages
library(data.table)  # fast data handling
library(fixest)      # high-dim FE + SunAbraham DID
library(did)         # Callaway & Sant’Anna estimator
library(ggplot2)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 1. Load data
dt <- fread("student_panel.csv")   # one row per student-year

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 2. Variable construction
# Adoption year at the school level
dt[, adopt_year := min(year[treatment_indicator == 1]), by = school_id]

# Ever treated dummy (needed by fixest SunAbraham)
dt[, ever_treated := !is.na(adopt_year)]

# Event time k (set NA for never treated)
dt[, k := ifelse(ever_treated, year - adopt_year, NA_integer_)]

# Main outcome
dt[, z_score := (test_score - mean(test_score, na.rm=TRUE)) /
                 sd(test_score, na.rm=TRUE), by = year]  # standardize by year

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 3. Main staggered DID (Sun & Abraham within fixest)
est_sa <- feols(z_score ~ sunab(adopt_year, year) |
                student_id + year,
                data = dt, cluster = ~school_id)

etable(est_sa, se = "cluster")

# Joint test for pre-trends
pretest <- linearHypothesis(est_sa, paste0("sunab::coefs::[-5:-1] = 0"))

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 4. Alternative estimator (Callaway–Sant’Anna)
cs <- att_gt(yname = "z_score",
             tname = "year",
             idname = "student_id",
             gname = "adopt_year",
             xformla = ~ gender + race + free_lunch,
             data = dt)
agg_effects <- aggte(cs, type = "dynamic")
summary(agg_effects)
ggdid(agg_effects)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
# 5. Robustness check: Placebo treatment in pre-period
dt[, placebo_year := adopt_year - 3]
dt[, pretend_treat := year >= placebo_year]

placebo <- feols(z_score ~ pretend_treat |
                 student_id + year,
                 data = dt[year < adopt_year], cluster = ~school_id)
etable(placebo)

# -----------------------------------------------------------
```

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

Theory/previous evidence suggests that better pedagogy and curricula raise
achievement. We therefore expect a positive impact:  

• Immediate (k = 0/1): +0.05–0.10 SD in test scores.  
• Medium run (k = 3): +0.20 SD.  
• Long run (k = 5+): +0.25–0.30 SD.

Knowledge retention should rise, leading to steeper cumulative gains than the
initial jump.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID)

C1. Parallel pre-trends visually and statistically verified ………………… 1  
C2. No anticipation behaviour prior to adoption ……………………………… 1  
C3. Stable unit composition over time (limited sorting) …………………… 0  
C4. No spillovers / SUTVA satisfied ………………………………………… 0  
C5. Common shocks controlled by year FE and covariates ………………… 1  

Total score = 3 / 5 → “moderately credible.” Future drafts will focus on
improving C3 and C4 through robustness and supplementary designs.

────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
